arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Ms. Cain argued that Congress included a provision delegating authority to the Attorney General for pre-enactment offenders.
Ms. Sherry stated that the Wetterling Act was not retroactive and did not apply to pre-enactment conduct.
The government advocate stated that the statute applies facially to all sex offenders regardless of conviction date.
Justice Scalia expressed concern about leaving the determination of criminal status to the Attorney General.

paragraphs: This case examines the scope of a federal registration mandate. The core issue is whether the law reaches past convictions or only future ones.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to rule that the registration law does not apply to pre-enactment convictions.
The government wants the Court to rule that the registration law applies to all sex offenders regardless of conviction date.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines whether federal registration mandates can reach individuals convicted before the law existed. It defines the temporal scope of criminal compliance requirements. It impacts how legislatures draft laws affecting past conduct. It clarifies the role of executive discretion in applying statutory mandates.
